term:A/B Testing.deep_dive: Two versions run simultaneously on split live traffic so their real-world performance can be compared statistically before committing to one. For AI deployment it doubles as a governance control: the incumbent keeps serving most users while the challenger proves itself on a controlled slice.
term:A/B Testing.exam_tip: Distinguish from shadow mode — in A/B testing both variants affect real users; in shadow mode the challenger's outputs affect no one.

term:AI Act Milestone — August 2, 2026.deep_dive: As originally enacted, this was the AI Act's general date of application, when the Annex III high-risk regime, the Article 50 transparency duties and the Commission's GPAI fining powers were all due to start. The 2026 Digital Omnibus kept 2 August 2026 as the general date but moved the high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I), and national sandboxes to 2 August 2027. What still starts on this date: Article 50 transparency, and Commission enforcement of GPAI obligations including Article 101 fines.
term:AI Act Milestone — August 2, 2026.exam_tip: Anchor check: 'as enacted', high-risk starts here; 'as amended by the 2026 Omnibus', only transparency and GPAI enforcement do.

term:AI Act Milestone — February 2, 2025.deep_dive: The first substantive AI Act deadline: prohibited practices (social scoring, exploitative manipulation, most real-time remote biometric ID) became illegal, and AI literacy expectations for provider and deployer staff took effect. It came only six months after entry into force — far faster than the rest of the Act.
term:AI Act Milestone — February 2, 2025.exam_tip: Two things attach to this date: prohibitions AND AI literacy — questions often test the second, lesser-known half.

term:AI Component.deep_dive: ISO/IEC 22989's building-block term: any functional element that makes up an AI system — a model, a data pipeline, a knowledge base, an inference engine. Governance attaches to the assembled system, but risk analysis has to decompose it into components because each fails differently.
term:AI Component.exam_tip: Component ⊂ system: an AI system is components plus interfaces, data flows, and operational context.

term:AI Customer.deep_dive: In the ISO 22989 role taxonomy, the party that acquires or receives an AI product or service — distinct from the provider who supplies it and the user who operates it. Role clarity matters because contractual risk allocation (warranties, audit rights, liability) follows these lines.
term:AI Customer.exam_tip: ISO roles (provider/producer/customer/user/subject) are not the EU AI Act roles (provider/deployer/importer/distributor) — keep the two vocabularies separate.

term:AI Distributor.deep_dive: An EU AI Act supply-chain role: an entity (other than provider or importer) that makes an AI system available on the EU market without changing it. Distributors must verify the system bears CE marking and required documentation, and must not supply systems they have reason to believe are non-compliant.
term:AI Distributor.exam_tip: Distributor = verify-and-pass-through; if it rebrands or substantially modifies the system, it becomes the provider with full provider duties.

term:AI Impact Assessment.deep_dive: The AI-specific look-before-you-leap: a structured evaluation of a system's potential effects on individuals, groups, organizations, and society — broader than a DPIA (not limited to personal data) and increasingly expected by frameworks (ISO 42001 requires one) and laws. Anatomy: describe the system, identify affected parties, rate severity and likelihood, mitigate, decide on residual risk, revisit.
term:AI Impact Assessment.exam_tip: AIIA covers social/ethical/legal impacts broadly; DPIA is the GDPR-mandated subset for personal-data risk — scope is the difference.

term:AI Importer.deep_dive: The EU AI Act role for bringing third-country AI into the Union: an EU-established entity placing a foreign provider's system on the EU market. Importers must verify conformity assessment was performed, documentation exists, and CE marking is affixed before the system enters the market.
term:AI Importer.exam_tip: Importers verify, they don't perform, conformity assessment — 'the importer must conduct the conformity assessment' is a wrong-answer pattern.

term:AI Management System (AIMS).deep_dive: The ISO/IEC 42001 construct: the interlocking set of policies, objectives, processes, roles, and controls through which an organization governs AI — analogous to an ISMS for security. Built on Annex SL and PDCA, it is the thing an auditor certifies: not any single model, but the organizational machine that manages all of them.
term:AI Management System (AIMS).exam_tip: Certification attaches to the management system, not to individual AI models — a certified AIMS doesn't make any given model 'certified safe.'

term:AI Manufacturer.deep_dive: In product-safety framing, the entity that produces an AI-enabled product and answers for its safety — the term matters where AI is a safety component of regulated products (machinery, medical devices, vehicles) and product legislation assigns duties to manufacturers. Under the AI Act, product manufacturers can inherit provider obligations when high-risk AI ships inside their products.
term:AI Manufacturer.exam_tip: AI embedded in a regulated product routes through both the product's sectoral law and the AI Act — manufacturers wear both hats.

term:AI Partner.deep_dive: A third party in the AI value chain that collaborates in developing, supplying, or operating AI capability — cloud platforms, model vendors, data suppliers, integrators. Partner risk is third-party risk: their training data, security posture, and model changes become your exposure without your visibility.
term:AI Partner.exam_tip: Whatever the partner does, accountability to regulators and affected individuals stays with the organization deploying the system.

term:AI Provider.deep_dive: The EU AI Act's central duty-bearer: the entity that develops an AI system (or has it developed) and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. Providers of high-risk systems own the heavyweight obligations — risk management, data governance, documentation, conformity assessment, CE marking, post-market monitoring.
term:AI Provider.exam_tip: Watch the role-shift trap: deployers who rebrand or substantially modify a high-risk system become providers and inherit everything.

term:AI Risk Sources (ISO 23894 Annex B).deep_dive: ISO 23894's informative catalog of where AI risk originates: data quality and availability, lack of explainability, degree of automation, system complexity, hardware and software faults, lifecycle and supply-chain factors, and the deployment environment. It functions as a completeness checklist when populating an AI risk register.
term:AI Risk Sources (ISO 23894 Annex B).exam_tip: Annex B = risk sources, Annex A = objectives, Annex C = lifecycle mapping — the three annexes are easily confused.

term:AI Subject.deep_dive: ISO 22989's term for the person affected by an AI system's operation — the loan applicant scored, the patient triaged, the pedestrian detected — who often never chose or touched the system. Governance frameworks exist substantially to protect this role: impact assessments, transparency, and contestability all point at the AI subject.
term:AI Subject.exam_tip: Parallel to GDPR's 'data subject' but broader — an AI subject need not have contributed any personal data to be affected.

term:Accountability.deep_dive: The principle that identifiable humans and organizations answer for AI outcomes — assignment of responsibility, obligation to explain and justify, and exposure to consequences. It is deliberately non-delegable: 'the algorithm decided' is the precise failure mode accountability frameworks exist to prevent.
term:Accountability.exam_tip: Accountability = who answers for it; responsibility = who does it — governance questions often hinge on keeping the accountable party human and named.

term:Accountable and Transparent.deep_dive: One of NIST AI RMF's seven trustworthiness characteristics: information about the system and its outputs is available to those who need it, and ownership of consequences is clear. NIST pairs the two because transparency without accountability is theater, and accountability without transparency is impossible to exercise.
term:Accountable and Transparent.exam_tip: Recognize the seven-characteristic list on sight: valid & reliable; safe; secure & resilient; accountable & transparent; explainable & interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair.

term:Activation Function.deep_dive: The nonlinear function applied to a neuron's weighted input sum that decides what signal passes onward — the nonlinearity (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) is what lets stacked layers learn non-linear patterns at all. Governance-level relevance: it's part of why neural networks resist human interpretation.
term:Activation Function.exam_tip: Know it as neural-network anatomy vocabulary — the exam tests recognition, not calculus.

term:Adversarial Example.deep_dive: An input crafted to make a model fail — perturbations often imperceptible to humans (a sticker on a stop sign, pixel noise on an image) that flip the model's output. Their existence is why security testing for AI includes adversarial robustness, not just conventional penetration testing.
term:Adversarial Example.exam_tip: Adversarial examples attack the model at inference time; data poisoning attacks it at training time — the timing distinction is tested.

term:Algorithmic Bias.deep_dive: Systematic unfairness in algorithmic outputs — sourced from unrepresentative training data, historically biased labels, proxy features, or feedback loops, and manifesting as disparate performance or outcomes across groups. It is a sociotechnical problem: the algorithm faithfully amplifies what the data and design gave it.
term:Algorithmic Bias.exam_tip: Bias can enter at every stage (data, features, labels, deployment) — answers locating it only in 'bad data' are incomplete.

term:Annex SL.deep_dive: ISO's harmonized high-level structure for management system standards — the shared clause skeleton (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement) that makes ISO 42001 dock cleanly with ISO 27001 and 9001. Organizations with an existing ISMS can extend it to AI rather than building parallel machinery.
term:Annex SL.exam_tip: Annex SL is why 'integrate the AIMS with existing management systems' is a realistic (and usually correct) answer.

term:Anonymization.deep_dive: Processing personal data so individuals can no longer be identified — by anyone, using reasonably likely means, irreversibly. Genuinely anonymous data exits GDPR scope, which is exactly why the bar is high: quasi-identifier combinations (age + zip + condition) and model-based attacks defeat naive 'we removed the names' claims.
term:Anonymization.exam_tip: If re-identification is reasonably possible, it was pseudonymization, not anonymization — and GDPR still applies in full.

term:Article 22 GDPR.deep_dive: The automated-decision article: individuals have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects. Exceptions (contract necessity, law, explicit consent) come with mandatory safeguards — at minimum human intervention, the ability to express a view, and to contest the decision.
term:Article 22 GDPR.exam_tip: 'Solely automated' is the hinge — genuine human review before the decision takes effect takes you outside Article 22.

term:Article 35 GDPR.deep_dive: The DPIA mandate: a data protection impact assessment is required where processing is likely to result in high risk to individuals — with systematic and extensive automated evaluation (profiling), large-scale special-category processing, and systematic public monitoring called out expressly. If the DPIA leaves risk high, Article 36 requires consulting the supervisory authority before processing.
term:Article 35 GDPR.exam_tip: AI profiling with significant effects is the textbook Article 35 trigger — and 'do a DPIA first' is a frequent correct answer.

term:Article 56 (EU AI Act).deep_dive: The provision authorizing codes of practice for GPAI: the AI Office facilitates multi-stakeholder codes that give providers a concrete path to demonstrating compliance with Articles 53 and 55. The 2025 GPAI Code of Practice is its product — a demonstration aid, expressly not a safe harbor.
term:Article 56 (EU AI Act).exam_tip: Article 56 = codes of practice; adherence eases the evidentiary burden but never constitutes conclusive proof of compliance.

term:Article 9 GDPR.deep_dive: The special-categories article: processing data revealing race/ethnicity, political opinions, religion, trade-union membership, genetic data, biometric data for identification, health, or sex life/orientation is prohibited unless one of the 9(2) conditions applies (explicit consent, employment law, vital interests, substantial public interest, etc.). AI multiplies exposure because models infer these categories from ordinary data.
term:Article 9 GDPR.exam_tip: Article 6 lawful basis AND an Article 9 condition are both required for special categories — one without the other fails.

term:Artificial Intelligence (AI).deep_dive: The umbrella discipline: machine-based systems performing tasks associated with human intelligence — learning, reasoning, perception, language. Regulatory definitions narrow it functionally (the EU AI Act/OECD 'infers from inputs to generate outputs' formulation) precisely so 'is this AI?' has a legal answer.
term:Artificial Intelligence (AI).exam_tip: Know both the conceptual definition and the OECD/EU functional one — the latter decides regulatory scope.

term:Audit.deep_dive: Systematic, independent, evidence-based examination against defined criteria — a framework, standard, regulation, or the organization's own policies. For AI: internal audits check the governance program, algorithmic audits probe specific properties (bias, robustness), and external certification audits (ISO 42001) provide third-party assurance.
term:Audit.exam_tip: Independence and defined criteria make an audit an audit — the builders reviewing their own system informally is monitoring, not audit.

term:Automatic Summarization.deep_dive: The NLP task of condensing text while preserving meaning — extractive (selecting key sentences) or abstractive (generating new phrasing). As an ISO 22989 catalog entry it illustrates task-specific narrow AI; in modern practice it's an LLM capability with hallucination risk attached to the abstractive variant.
term:Automatic Summarization.exam_tip: One of the ISO 22989 NLP task definitions — recognize it as terminology rather than a governance concept.

term:Availability.deep_dive: The security-triad property that systems and data are accessible when needed. For AI it extends to model serving (inference uptime), data pipeline continuity, and graceful degradation — an unavailable safety-critical model is itself a safety incident.
term:Availability.exam_tip: CIA triad member — availability failures in AI scenarios are security/resilience issues, not performance tuning.

term:Bayesian Network.deep_dive: A probabilistic graphical model encoding variables and their conditional dependencies as a directed acyclic graph — reasoning under uncertainty with explicit, inspectable probability structure. Governance-relevant because it's a naturally more interpretable model family than deep networks.
term:Bayesian Network.exam_tip: Recognize as a classic/symbolic-adjacent, relatively explainable ML technique — a contrast point to black-box deep learning.

term:Benchmarking.deep_dive: Evaluating a model against standardized datasets or tasks to compare performance across models or over time. The governance caveat is benchmark gaming and distribution mismatch: excellent benchmark scores prove little about behavior on your population — which is why ARIA-style realistic evaluation exists.
term:Benchmarking.exam_tip: 'It scored well on benchmarks' never substitutes for validation on the deployment population.

term:Bias (Systematic Deviation).deep_dive: The ISO-flavored definition: systematic deviation from a true value or fair outcome — encompassing statistical bias (estimation error), computational bias, and the human/social biases that data absorbs. NIST SP 1270 organizes it in three categories: systemic, computational/statistical, and human-cognitive.
term:Bias (Systematic Deviation).exam_tip: Bias is not only prejudice — statistical deviation counts too; the NIST three-category taxonomy is the tested structure.

term:Bias Testing.deep_dive: Empirically measuring model performance and outcomes across demographic slices — error rates, positive rates, and calibration per group, compared against fairness metrics chosen for the context. It requires access to (or sound inference of) sensitive attributes, which is why governed access beats attribute deletion.
term:Bias Testing.exam_tip: Bias testing compares subgroup performance — overall accuracy alone can hide a 10-point gap between groups.

term:Biometric Data.deep_dive: Personal data from technical processing of physical, physiological, or behavioral characteristics — faceprints, fingerprints, voiceprints, gait. Under GDPR it becomes special-category when used to uniquely identify someone; under the AI Act, biometric use cases populate both the prohibited list (untargeted scraping, real-time remote ID) and Annex III high-risk categories.
term:Biometric Data.exam_tip: A photo is not special-category biometric data; a faceprint template used for identification is — the processing purpose flips the category.

term:Breach Notification.deep_dive: GDPR's clock-driven duty: personal data breaches go to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of awareness (Art 33) and to affected individuals without undue delay when risk is high (Art 34). AI adds novel breach shapes — model inversion or membership inference can constitute disclosure of personal data without any database being touched.
term:Breach Notification.exam_tip: 72 hours to the authority; individuals only when high risk — and remember parallel AI Act incident-reporting clocks can run simultaneously.

term:Brittleness.deep_dive: AI's tendency to fail abruptly and completely when conditions deviate slightly from training experience — the opposite of the graceful degradation engineering aims for. Brittleness is why edge-case and robustness testing exist, and why confident model output in unfamiliar territory is a hazard.
term:Brittleness.exam_tip: Brittleness = catastrophic failure on small distribution shifts; robustness is its antonym and the design goal.

term:Business Context.deep_dive: The organizational reality an AI system serves: objectives, sector, risk appetite, regulatory exposure, and the workflows it lives inside. Context determines proportionality — identical models warrant different governance in ad targeting versus clinical triage — and grounding systems in defined business context is the first design-phase control.
term:Business Context.exam_tip: ISO 42001's 'context of the organization' clause institutionalizes this — governance is always calibrated to context, never one-size.

term:Business Objectives.deep_dive: The measurable outcomes an AI initiative exists to achieve — defined before development so success criteria, validation thresholds, and monitoring targets have something to anchor to. Objectives also bound scope: a system approved to reduce fraud losses was not approved to screen employees.
term:Business Objectives.exam_tip: Success criteria defined up front enable everything downstream — their absence is the root cause in many 'what went wrong' scenarios.

term:CE Marking.deep_dive: The EU's conformity mark: affixing it declares a high-risk AI system has passed conformity assessment against the AI Act's requirements, making it eligible for the EU market. It's the visible end of an evidentiary chain — risk management, data governance, technical documentation, assessment — that authorities can unwind on inspection.
term:CE Marking.exam_tip: Sequence matters: conformity assessment → CE marking → market placement; importers and distributors verify the mark exists.

term:Choice.deep_dive: The privacy principle of giving individuals meaningful options over their data — consent where required, opt-outs where offered, and honored preferences either way. AI strains it because downstream training uses are hard to explain at collection time, and choice given but ignored is worse than no choice at all.
term:Choice.exam_tip: Notice tells; choice empowers — an exam scenario offering buried, illusory, or coerced options is testing whether the choice was meaningful.

term:Classic AI.deep_dive: The symbolic, rule-based tradition — knowledge encoded as explicit rules and logic (expert systems, search, planning) rather than learned from data. Its governance virtue is transparency: the rules can be read. Its limitation — brittleness outside coded knowledge — is what machine learning displaced.
term:Classic AI.exam_tip: Symbolic/classic AI = hand-coded rules, explainable; connectionist/ML = learned patterns, opaque — a recurring contrast pair.

term:Cognitive Computing.deep_dive: A largely marketing-era label for systems that simulate human thought processes — perception, reasoning, natural language — popularized around IBM Watson. In taxonomy terms it gestures at the same territory as AI broadly; treat it as vocabulary rather than a distinct technology.
term:Cognitive Computing.exam_tip: Recognize the synonym; don't over-analyze — it's tested as terminology awareness.

term:Competent Authorities.deep_dive: The bodies each EU member state designates to supervise and enforce the AI Act — notifying authorities (overseeing conformity-assessment bodies) and market surveillance authorities (investigating systems, ordering corrective action, imposing penalties). They anchor national enforcement while the AI Office handles GPAI at Union level.
term:Competent Authorities.exam_tip: National authorities enforce against most systems; the European AI Office supervises GPAI — jurisdiction questions split along that line.

term:Computer Vision.deep_dive: The AI field enabling machines to derive meaning from images and video — classification, detection, segmentation, recognition. Governance flashpoints: facial recognition (biometric identification law), surveillance proportionality, and safety-critical perception in vehicles and medicine.
term:Computer Vision.exam_tip: When a scenario involves cameras identifying people, jump to biometric/special-category analysis and the AI Act's biometric restrictions.

term:Concept Drift.deep_dive: The world changing under the model: the relationship between inputs and outputs shifts (fraud patterns evolve, consumer behavior changes), so a model trained on yesterday's relationship degrades even if input data looks the same. Detection needs outcome monitoring, and the remedy is retraining on current reality.
term:Concept Drift.exam_tip: Concept drift = input→output relationship changes; data drift = input distribution changes — the exam tests the distinction precisely.

term:Confabulation.deep_dive: NIST AI 600-1's formal term for hallucination: generative models producing confidently stated, plausible, false content — a structural property of next-token prediction, not an occasional bug. Governance responses: grounding (RAG), verification workflows for consequential uses, user training against over-trust, and honest capability communication.
term:Confabulation.exam_tip: Confabulation/hallucination is the signature GAI risk — listed first among AI 600-1's twelve; 'the model never errs' options are automatically wrong.

term:Conformity Assessment.deep_dive: The EU AI Act's pre-market verification: demonstrating a high-risk system meets Chapter III requirements — via internal control for most Annex III categories, or a notified body for certain cases (notably biometrics). It produces the evidence chain behind the CE mark, and must be repeated after substantial modification.
term:Conformity Assessment.exam_tip: Most high-risk systems allow provider self-assessment (internal control); third-party notified-body assessment is the exception, not the rule.

term:Conformity Requirements.deep_dive: The substantive bar a high-risk system must clear: risk management system, data governance and quality, technical documentation (Annex IV), record-keeping/logging, transparency and instructions for use, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity. Conformity assessment verifies these; CE marking declares them.
term:Conformity Requirements.exam_tip: Learn the requirement set as a chain — exam questions ask which link is missing in a scenario.

term:Connectionism (Connectionist Paradi.deep_dive: The intelligence-from-networks school: cognition emerging from many simple connected units with learned weights — the paradigm behind neural networks and deep learning, standing opposite symbolic AI's explicit rules. Its triumph is capability; its governance cost is opacity.
term:Connectionism (Connectionist Paradi.exam_tip: Connectionist = subsymbolic = neural — three labels for the learned-weights paradigm, contrasted with symbolic/rule-based AI.

term:Consent.deep_dive: GDPR's most demanding lawful basis: freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, given by clear affirmative act, withdrawable as easily as given — with the burden of proof on the controller. For AI training it's often the wrong tool (hard to make specific and informed for future model uses), which is why compatibility analysis and other bases get exam attention.
term:Consent.exam_tip: Test each adjective: bundled (not specific), buried (not informed), or forced (not free) consent fails — and consent is one of six bases, not the default.
